title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
description: Brute force to optimized: storing one list's nodes in a set versus two pointers that switch lists upon reaching the end, equalizing length differences.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the heads of two singly linked lists headA and headB, return the node at which the two lists intersect (share the exact same node onward), or null if the two lists do not intersect.

blocks.caption: Two pointers, each switching to the other list once they reach the end of their own

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Two lists may share a common TAIL, of unknown alignment","The two lists have different \"extra\" lengths before that shared tail begins; equalizing this difference is the key challenge"],["An O(1) space solution is explicitly desired, without pre-computing either list's length","Two pointers, each redirected to the OTHER list's head once they reach their own list's end, naturally equalize the length difference over one combined pass"],["Comparing NODE IDENTITY (not value) matters, since two different nodes could coincidentally share the same value","Pointer/reference equality must be used for the comparison, not a value comparison"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given two singly linked lists that might share a common tail (the exact same nodes from some point onward), find the first shared node, or determine that no such intersection exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Roads Merging Into One Shared Final Stretch
blocks.text: Like two separate roads of different lengths that eventually merge into the exact same final stretch of highway. Two drivers, one starting on each road, and each driver, upon reaching the end of their own road, immediately continues onto the START of the OTHER road instead; since together they now drive the combined total distance of both roads exactly once each, they're guaranteed to arrive at the merge point (if one exists) at the exact same moment.

blocks.caption: Redirecting each pointer to the other list's head exactly equalizes the two lists' differing lengths

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: listA-only = [4,1], listB-only = [5,6,1], shared tail = [8,4,5]

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before computing each list's exact length to figure out how to align them, notice that redirecting each pointer to the other list's head, upon reaching its own end, automatically equalizes any length difference.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the two lists intersect, they share some common tail, meaning listA's length equals (listA's unique prefix) + (shared tail), and similarly for listB; the two lists' unique prefixes may differ in length.

Observation 2: Two pointers starting at headA and headB respectively, each walking forward normally, would reach the shared tail at DIFFERENT times if the unique prefixes have different lengths, making a naive simultaneous walk fail to detect the intersection directly.

Observation 3: If, upon reaching the end of its own list (null), a pointer is redirected to the START of the OTHER list, then by the time both pointers have each walked their own full list once and the other list's prefix, they will have each covered the exact same TOTAL distance (lenA + lenB), landing them on the same node at the same time.

Observation 4: If the lists genuinely intersect, this guarantees the two pointers meet exactly at the intersection node; if they don't intersect, both pointers simply reach null (undefined/None) at the exact same moment, which is detected by the same equality check.

Recognizing that redirecting each pointer to the OTHER list's head exactly compensates for any length difference between the two lists, without ever needing to compute either length explicitly, is the elegant core insight here.

This is a two-pointer technique that cleverly equalizes an unknown length difference between two sequences by having each pointer walk BOTH sequences (in a different order), guaranteeing they cover the same total distance.
6. Brute Force Solution
Store every node from list A in a set, then walk through list B checking whether each of its nodes already appears in that set.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk through list A, storing every node (by reference/identity) in a set.
Walk through list B; the first node found to already be in the set is the intersection node.

codes.python:
def get_intersection_node(headA, headB):
    nodes_in_a = set()
    node = headA
    while node:
        nodes_in_a.add(id(node))                                           # remember every node object in list A
        node = node.next
    node = headB
    while node:
        if id(node) in nodes_in_a:                                         # the first node from B also in A is the intersection
            return node
        node = node.next
    return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    common = ListNode(8, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))
    headA = ListNode(4, ListNode(1, common))
    headB = ListNode(5, ListNode(6, ListNode(1, common)))
    result = get_intersection_node(headA, headB)
    print(result.val if result else None)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The set stores node identities (references/pointers), not values, since the intersection must be the exact same node object, not merely a coincidentally equal value.
List A is fully processed first, since the set needs to be completely built before list B can be checked against it.
The function returns the first matching node found while walking list B, which is guaranteed to be the true intersection point.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every node of list B is checked against the complete set of list A's nodes, so the true intersection (if any) is always correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), where m and n are the lengths of the two lists.
Space: O(m), for storing every node of list A in the set.

Limitation: storing every node of one list in a set uses O(m) extra space, when a clever two-pointer technique (redirecting each pointer to the other list once it reaches its own end) can find the exact same intersection using only O(1) extra space.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force stores an entire list's nodes in a set. Instead, use two pointers, pA starting at headA and pB starting at headB. Advance each by one node per step; whenever a pointer reaches the end of its own list (becomes null), redirect it to the START of the OTHER list instead of stopping. Continue until the two pointers point to the exact same node (the intersection) or both simultaneously become null (no intersection).

Initialize pA to headA and pB to headB. While pA is not the same node as pB, advance each: if pA is null, set it to headB, otherwise advance it to pA.next (and symmetrically for pB with headA). Return pA once the loop ends, whether that's the intersection node or null.
9. Optimized Solution
Two pointers walk their own list then the other's, guaranteeing they cover equal total distance and meet at the intersection.
Dry run for listA-only=[4,1], listB-only=[5,6,1], shared tail=[8,4,5] (listA length 5, listB length 6)

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Both pointers land on the node valued 8 at step 9, correctly identifying the intersection.

codes.python:
def get_intersection_node(headA, headB):
    p_a, p_b = headA, headB
    while p_a is not p_b:
        p_a = headB if p_a is None else p_a.next                           # once A's pointer runs out, redirect it to B's head
        p_b = headA if p_b is None else p_b.next                           # once B's pointer runs out, redirect it to A's head
    return p_a                                                              # they meet at the intersection, or both become None together


if __name__ == "__main__":
    common = ListNode(8, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))
    headA = ListNode(4, ListNode(1, common))
    headB = ListNode(5, ListNode(6, ListNode(1, common)))
    result = get_intersection_node(headA, headB)
    print(result.val if result else None)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), since each pointer traverses at most its own list plus the other list once.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the 2 pointer variables.
Why This Works

By the time both pointers have each traversed their own list once, plus however much of the other list they've covered, they will have BOTH walked exactly (length of A + length of B) nodes total. If an intersection exists at some point, both pointers arrive at that exact node simultaneously, since the "extra" unique-prefix length difference between the two lists gets exactly compensated for by this redirect-to-the-other-list mechanism. If no intersection exists, both pointers simply reach null at exactly the same step (having each traversed the full combined length), satisfying the same termination check.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The pA == pB comparison checks node IDENTITY (reference/pointer equality), correctly distinguishing a true intersection from merely coincidentally equal values.
The redirect logic (pA = pA == null ? headB : pA.next) elegantly combines "keep advancing normally" and "switch to the other list" into a single line.
Returning pA (rather than pB) is arbitrary but sufficient, since by the time the loop ends, both pointers point to the exact same node (or both are null).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The "redirect each pointer to the other sequence's start" technique is a broadly elegant way to equalize an unknown length difference between two sequences without ever computing either length explicitly, guaranteeing both pointers cover the exact same total distance.
Common mistakes

items: Comparing node VALUES instead of node references/identities, which would incorrectly report an "intersection" whenever two unrelated nodes happen to share the same value.
Forgetting to redirect a pointer to the OTHER list's head when it reaches null, instead simply stopping, which breaks the length-equalizing guarantee.
Assuming both lists must have the same length before intersecting, which isn't required at all; the technique works correctly regardless of how different the two "unique prefix" lengths are.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly explain WHY redirecting each pointer to the other list's head equalizes any length difference (both pointers end up covering length A + length B total, regardless of how that's split between the two lists), since this justification is the elegant core of the solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find where two linked lists intersect, using O(1) space, without knowing their lengths" points toward the two-pointer technique where each pointer switches to the other list upon reaching its own end.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you solve this if you were allowed to compute each list's length first? Compute both lengths, advance the pointer of the longer list by the length difference first, then walk both pointers together in lockstep until they match, an equivalent but less elegant approach.
How would this change for DOUBLY linked lists? The core two-pointer redirect technique still applies identically, since it only relies on forward traversal.

What if the lists could have a cycle as well as an intersection? This combination would require first detecting and handling any cycles (via Floyd's algorithm) before this intersection technique could be safely applied, since an infinite loop could otherwise occur.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A distinctive two-pointer technique, different in spirit from the classic slow/fast speed-ratio pointers seen in Linked List Cycle and Middle of the Linked List, instead using a "switch lists upon reaching the end" trick to equalize length differences.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m + n) time, O(m) space.
Optimized (two pointers, redirect to the other list): O(m + n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Two pointers, each redirected to the OTHER list's head upon reaching the end of its own
Core Idea: By the time both pointers have traversed length A + length B total nodes, they must meet at the intersection (or both reach null together)
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Redirecting each pointer to the other list's head exactly equalizes any unknown length difference, without ever computing either list's length
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: pA = pA ? pA.next : headB; pB = pB ? pB.next : headA; they meet at the intersection
